Numerical Control (NC) machine [U1·S6, S7, S9]
 Programmable automation for machining; movements are controlled by numerical codes stored in alphanumeric form (G-
 codes and M-codes).
 Programs can be modified and reused; gives high precision and consistent quality; reduces manual intervention and human
 error.
 Working principle: part program prepared in numerical codes → fed to the NC controller → controller interprets the
 commands → machine controls tool movement, spindle speed and feed rate automatically → component produced with high
 accuracy and repeatability.

Five main components of an NC machine (S7): (1) Machine Control Unit (MCU) interprets the program and machine movements;
(2) Input device transfers the machining program to the controller; (3) Machine tool performs the cutting; (4) Drive system
controls axis movements and spindle rotation; (5) Feedback system (closed-loop NC) monitors and corrects positioning errors.




 Main components of an NC machine and flow of operation. From Unit 1 slides, S7.


Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine [U1·S8]

 A CNC machine is an advanced form of NC in which a microcomputer-based Machine Control Unit (MCU) controls machine-
 tool operations automatically using programmed instructions.


Why CNC: higher flexibility and automation; faster processing and improved accuracy; easy program storage and editing; better
productivity and reliability (also: reduced lead time, reduced scrap rate, consistent quality, reduced manpower). Flow: Part
program → MCU → Servo drives → Machine tool → Finished component.




 Challenges in CNC machining (a cup). From Unit 1 slides, S10.


Challenges in CNC machining (cup example, S10): the cavity may be too deep to machine; the undercut cannot be machined
without more than a 3-axis machine; the base cannot be machined without holding it in a fixture; sharp internal features cannot
be machined without a tool radius. These limits are exactly where AM is strong.

 1.2 What is Additive Manufacturing? Definition and history

 Additive Manufacturing (AM), commonly known as 3D printing, is the process of making objects layer by layer directly from
 a 3D CAD model; material is added, not removed. [U1·S13]


 Can produce complex shapes with ease; reduces material waste; removes many limitations of conventional manufacturing.
 Supports rapid prototyping and low-volume production.
 Shifts the focus from Design for Manufacturing (DFM) to Manufacturing for Design (MFD) — the part design is no longer bent
 around what the process can make.

History [U1·S2]
 The earliest 3D-printing technologies first became visible in the late 1980s, when they were called Rapid Prototyping (RP).
 They were conceived as a fast, cost-effective way to create prototypes for product development.
 1983 — Charles “Chuck” Hull invents Stereolithography (SLA), a technology that creates solid objects from a CAD/CAM file; he
 coined the term “stereolithography”. SLA cures and solidifies successive layers of liquid photopolymer resin using an ultraviolet
 laser. Hull founded 3D Systems; the slide shows the first AM machine.
 The field came to be called variously “additive manufacturing”, “rapid prototyping” and “3D printing”.

Step Explanation

 manipulation

 4. Machine setup Set process parameters (layer thickness, nozzle/laser settings, temperatures, infill, speed), load material and
 prepare the build platform.

 5. Build The machine builds the part layer by layer, mostly unattended, until the last layer.

 6. Removal Take the part off the platform; remove loose powder / uncured resin; separate from base plate.

 7. Post-processing Remove supports, clean, sand/polish, cure, heat-treat, paint, etc.

Model slicing [U1·S55–S57]

 Slicing is the act of converting a 3D model into a set of instructions for the 3D printer. It “slices” the model into thin layers and
 determines how each layer is printed (the tool path) to obtain minimum time, best strength, etc. A slicer takes a 3D CAD
 model — generally an STL file — and converts it into G-code that gives commands to the printer.


 Slicing is the foundational operation of 3D printing; it requires computing the intersection curves of the model and the slicing
 planes.
 It is time-consuming and a key factor affecting printing quality.
 Most slicing algorithms work on STL (standard tessellation language) models. STL data is a discretized form of the 3D model, so
 it contains discretization errors; many studies therefore slice directly on the original CAD data.

Three types of slicer settings (S57): Print settings — layer height, shells, infill per cent, speed; Filament settings — filament
diameter, extrusion multiplier, extruder temperature, print-bed temperature; Printer settings — nozzle diameter, print-bed shape
